stories.issue: Should India deepen alignment with the US even if it narrows room for strategic autonomy?
stories.title: India balances strategic autonomy with closer US ties
stories.whatIsHappening: India and the US are working more closely on trade, technology and security while continuing to manage disagreements over market access and foreign-policy priorities.
stories.argument: Closer partnership can provide access to technology, investment and supply-chain alternatives while balancing China’s influence.
stories.otherSide: India’s economic and diplomatic interests are not identical to Washington’s, and over-alignment could make independent decisions harder.
stories.whyItMatters: The relationship affects investment, defence technology, supply chains and India’s ability to shape a multipolar order. For Indian businesses, closer ties can open markets and capital, but dependence on one bloc can reduce room to manoeuvre.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: The useful lens is not simply friend or rival. Ask which issue areas benefit from alignment, which require flexibility, and whether India’s domestic capability is strong enough to make autonomy meaningful.
keyFacts: The US is one of India’s largest trading and investment partners.
Defence, critical technology and supply-chain resilience are central to the relationship.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Can India build a stronger India–US partnership without giving up strategic autonomy?

stories.issue: How vulnerable is India to a prolonged oil shock?
stories.title: Oil shock risk keeps inflation and growth in tension
stories.whatIsHappening: Geopolitical uncertainty has kept energy markets volatile, with investors watching supply risks, shipping routes and the duration of any disruption.
stories.argument: A prolonged shock can justify cushioning households and businesses because energy costs pass through transport, fertiliser and manufacturing.
stories.otherSide: Broad price support can protect consumers in the short term while worsening fiscal pressure and weakening incentives to conserve energy.
stories.whyItMatters: India imports most of the crude it consumes, so a sustained rise can pressure inflation, the rupee and the current account. It also complicates the choices facing the government and the RBI.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Separate a short disruption from a long one. The answer depends on who absorbs the cost, how long prices remain high, whether domestic producers benefit, and how quickly energy diversification can reduce exposure.
keyFacts: Crude oil is India’s largest import item by value in many years.
The impact depends heavily on how long prices stay elevated, not only on the peak price.
Oil prices influence inflation, the rupee and India’s trade balance together.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: What should India prioritise if oil prices stay high for a year: growth, inflation control or fiscal support?

stories.issue: Can countries make supply chains resilient without making them permanently more expensive?
stories.title: Trade policy is becoming industrial policy
stories.whatIsHappening: Governments are using tariffs, export controls and subsidies to protect strategic industries and reduce dependence on concentrated supply chains.
stories.argument: Some redundancy is rational when disruption in chips, energy or critical inputs would impose very large economic and security costs.
stories.otherSide: Protection can raise costs, duplicate capacity and shield domestic firms from the competitive pressure needed to become efficient.
stories.whyItMatters: Companies are redesigning where they source, manufacture and hold inventory. The result could be more resilient systems, but also higher costs and a less predictable environment for cross-border investment.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Distinguish targeted resilience in genuinely strategic sectors from broad protectionism. The central trade-off is between paying for insurance today and preserving efficiency, openness and scale.
keyFacts: Semiconductors, energy and critical minerals are now treated as strategic assets.
China-plus-one diversifies risk but rarely replaces China’s scale and ecosystem quickly.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: When does supply-chain resilience become inefficient protectionism?

stories.issue: How should India balance rapid decarbonisation with affordable, reliable energy?
stories.title: India’s energy transition is a sequencing problem
stories.whatIsHappening: India is expanding renewable power and clean-energy investment while demand for electricity, transport and industrial energy continues to grow.
stories.argument: Faster clean-energy investment can reduce long-run fuel exposure, improve public health and build an industrial advantage in new energy systems.
stories.otherSide: Moving too quickly without reliable alternatives can make power costlier and weaken industrial growth, especially while electricity demand is rising.
stories.whyItMatters: The transition shapes competitiveness, energy security, jobs and public health. The difficult question is not whether to transition, but how to sequence investment, reliability and affordability.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Renewables require storage, transmission and flexible backup. A fair transition must also account for workers, states and households whose costs and livelihoods change.
keyFacts: India’s electricity demand is expected to keep rising as incomes and electrification increase.
Transmission, storage and financing are as important as generation capacity.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Should India prioritise the speed of emissions reduction or the affordability and reliability of energy?

stories.issue: Will AI create broad productivity gains or concentrate value in a few firms?
stories.title: AI adoption moves from pilots to operating-model choices
stories.whatIsHappening: Companies are moving generative AI beyond experiments into customer service, software development and internal workflows while weighing data, skills and governance costs.
stories.argument: Early adopters can gain speed and lower unit costs, and India could benefit as an application and services hub.
stories.otherSide: Displacement may arrive before new roles and training systems are ready, while value may accrue to platforms with data and distribution.
stories.whyItMatters: The biggest effect may come from how organisations redesign work, not from model capability alone. The distribution of productivity gains will matter as much as the gains themselves.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Ask who captures the productivity gain, who bears the transition cost, whether smaller firms can adopt responsibly, and what policy makes the gains broader.
keyFacts: AI adoption is moving fastest where workflows are measurable and repetitive.
India’s strengths include software talent, digital public infrastructure and large multilingual markets.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: What would make AI-led productivity growth inclusive rather than merely profitable?

extempore.issue: Should India prioritise strategic autonomy even when deeper economic alignment could deliver faster growth?
extempore.whyNow: India’s partnerships, trade choices and supply-chain decisions are being reshaped by geopolitical competition, energy risk and a more protectionist global economy.
argumentsFor: More flexibility lets India work with different blocs on different issues and preserve independent foreign-policy choices.
Diversified relationships can reduce the cost of dependence on one market, supplier or security partner.
Strategic autonomy can strengthen India’s bargaining power if backed by domestic capability.
argumentsAgainst: Closer alignment can bring faster access to capital, technology, markets and security cooperation.
Trying to remain equidistant can delay decisions when a crisis requires a clear choice.
Domestic self-reliance can become expensive protectionism if it is not tied to competitiveness and scale.
examples: India’s effort to attract electronics and semiconductor supply chains while keeping multiple diplomatic channels open.
The energy trade-off: importing affordable fuel today while investing in domestic renewables for resilience tomorrow.
facts: India’s largest strategic relationships span trade, technology, defence and energy rather than one single category.
Supply-chain diversification usually adds short-term cost before it reduces long-term risk.
The best policy can differ by sector: security-sensitive technology may need more autonomy than commodity trade.
